title: Thermal evolution of energy budgets and oxidative damage associated with a faster pace‐of‐life differs between larvae and adults in a range expanding damselfly
content:
Our study investigates the physiological traits underlying the evolution of a faster pace-of-life in a range-expanding damselfly and how these differ between larvae and adults. We show that faster pace-of-life evolution is associated with increased net energy budgets rather than oxidative stress, with these patterns differing between life stages.


Abstract

During range expansion, species may face warmer temperatures causing evolution of traits and their plasticity, including evolution of a faster pace-of-life (POL). The associated physiological trait changes remain poorly studied, especially to what extent these differ between larval and adult life stages. We studied the range expansion of the damselfly Ischnura elegans from southern France into two warmer regions of Spain: a ‘new edge’ region and an ‘old edge’ region (established ~13 and ~75 years ago, respectively). In a common garden experiment, larvae and adults from all three regions were reared from the egg stage under mean summer temperatures of Southern France (24°C) and Spain (28°C). The evolution of a higher net energy budget contributed to the evolution of a faster POL in the old edge Spanish larvae. In contrast, larvae from the new edge Spanish region, which did not evolve a faster POL, did not show an evolutionary increase in the net energy budget. Counter to general belief, the evolution of a faster POL was not associated with increased oxidative damage. This may explain why the evolution of a faster larval POL was not associated with a shortened adult lifespan. Thermal plasticity and evolution of physiology differed between life stages. Warming only caused the expected reduction in net energy budget in adults, and while both larvae and adults showed the expected increase in oxidative damage, this was more pronounced in adults, indicating terrestrial adults to be more sensitive to warming than aquatic larvae. In contrast with the larvae, the adults of the old edge Spanish region evolved a lower net energy budget suggesting energetic carry-over costs of their faster larval POL. Our research revealed evolutionary changes in the net energy budget and oxidative stress physiology and their thermal plasticity associated with the evolution of a faster POL and the higher temperatures encountered during a range expansion towards warmer regions. Notably, these patterns differed between both life stages, and evolutionary increases in the net energy budget, rather than oxidative stress physiology, explained the rapid POL evolution.
